title: 02. Data Structures: 09 — Comprehensions (Deep Dive)
summary: Comprehensions = compact, expressive way to build lists/dicts/sets/generators from iterables. They generate cleaner bytecode than explicit for + append and read like math.
objectives: if filter vs if/else expression — the famous confusion

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Comprehensions = compact, expressive way to build lists/dicts/sets/generators from iterables. They generate cleaner bytecode than explicit `for + append` and read like math.

sections.title: 1. The four forms
sections.body:
```python
# list — eager, in memory
squares = [x*x for x in range(10)]

# set — eager, deduplicates
unique = {c.lower() for c in text if c.isalpha()}

# dict — eager
sq = {x: x*x for x in range(10)}

# generator — LAZY, single-use
gen = (x*x for x in range(10))
sum(x*x for x in range(10**7))            # parens omitted as sole arg
```

There is **no tuple comprehension**. `(x for x in ...)` is a generator. Use `tuple(... for ...)`.

sections.title: 2. Anatomy
sections.body:
```python
[<expression> for <var> in <iterable> if <condition>]
```

- `<expression>` — what to put in the result.
- `if` — filter (after the `for`).
- Multiple `for` clauses → nested loops, leftmost is outermost.
- Multiple `if` clauses → ANDed.

```python
# pairs i,j with i != j
[(i,j) for i in range(3) for j in range(3) if i != j]

# nested with dependent iterables
[(i,j) for i in range(3) for j in range(i)]
```

sections.title: 3. if filter vs if/else expression — the famous confusion
sections.body:
```python
# Filter — keeps positives
[x for x in xs if x > 0]

# Map with branch — keeps everything, transforms
[x if x > 0 else 0 for x in xs]
```

The filter `if` goes **after the for**; the conditional expression `if/else` goes **inside the value**.

You can combine:

```python
[x*2 if x > 0 else 0 for x in xs if x is not None]
```

sections.title: 4. Nested comprehensions
sections.body:
### Flatten matrix

```python
flat = [v for row in matrix for v in row]
```

### Build a matrix

```python
m = [[i*j for j in range(5)] for i in range(5)]
```

### Transpose

```python
t = [list(col) for col in zip(*matrix)]
```

Read nested comprehensions outside-in: `[ <expr-item> for <outer> for <inner> ]`.

sections.title: 5. Generator expressions — laziness
sections.body:
```python
gen = (x*x for x in range(10**7))
print(next(gen))                          # 0
print(sum(gen))                           # consumes the rest
print(sum(gen))                           # 0 — already exhausted!
```

Use cases:

- Aggregations: `sum`, `any`, `all`, `min`, `max`, `max(..., key=...)`.
- Streaming pipelines (no intermediate lists).
- Memory-bound work.

When sole argument, parentheses are optional:

```python
any(x > 100 for x in nums)
", ".join(str(x) for x in xs)
```

sections.title: 6. Walrus := inside comprehensions (3.8+)
sections.body:
Avoid calling expensive function twice.

```python
[y for x in data if (y := f(x)) > 0]
# y is bound for use in the result expression and visible after (in same scope)
```

sections.title: 7. Scope behavior
sections.body:
- Comprehensions have their own scope (Py3) — loop variable doesn't leak.
- A normal `for` loop **does** leak its variable.

```python
[i for i in range(3)]
# i is NOT defined here
for i in range(3): pass
# i == 2 here
```

sections.title: 8. Performance & readability
sections.body:
- Comprehensions are typically **faster** than explicit `for + append` (optimized bytecode, fewer attr lookups).
- For large data, prefer **generator expressions** to avoid building intermediate lists.
- For simple work that's a built-in (`sum`, `map`), use the built-in directly:
  ```python
  total = sum(x*x for x in xs)
  ```
- Don't nest 3+ `for` clauses — switch to a regular loop for readability.
- Avoid side effects inside comprehensions — they should produce data, not log/print.

### Bench rough numbers (10M ints)

| Form                        | Time-ish                  |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `for + append`              | 1.0×                      |
| list comprehension          | ~0.7×                     |
| `map()` (built-in callable) | ~0.6×                     |
| `np.array(...)+something`   | order of magnitude faster |

sections.title: 9. Dict / set comprehension patterns
sections.body:
### Invert a dict

```python
inv = {v: k for k, v in d.items()}
```

### Index by attribute

```python
by_id = {u.id: u for u in users}
```

### Filter dict by value

```python
positive = {k: v for k, v in d.items() if v > 0}
```

### Group with dict comp + Counter (often simpler with `defaultdict`)

```python
{k: sum(x.amount for x in v) for k, v in groups.items()}
```

sections.title: 10. Common patterns
sections.body:
### Unique while preserving order

```python
seen = set()
out = [x for x in xs if not (x in seen or seen.add(x))]
# clever but ugly — explicit loop reads better
```

### Cartesian product

```python
[(a, b) for a in A for b in B]
# or
import itertools; list(itertools.product(A, B))
```

### Conditional flatten

```python
[v for row in matrix for v in row if v is not None]
```

### Read file lines into list of stripped non-empty

```python
with open("f") as f:
    lines = [ln.strip() for ln in f if ln.strip()]
```

### Counting via comprehension

```python
sum(1 for x in xs if predicate(x))
```

sections.title: 11. Anti-patterns
sections.body:
- Side effects inside (`[print(x) for x in xs]`).
- Triple+ nested loops in one comprehension.
- Hiding complex logic behind a one-liner.
- Mutating the iterable being iterated.
